segments.source: Civic institutions divide responsibilities. A problem can be solved by matching an action to a clearly defined function.
Given facts.

Roles are defined as follows: Town Council makes local policy and approves the budget; Public Works Office maintains roads; Local Court decides legal disputes; Election Committee administers elections; School Board sets school policies. A resident asks which institution should decide a dispute under law. Cross-domain check: a local committee has 15 members, requires at least 8 present for quorum, and 14 are present.
Rules.

Match the requested action to the stated role. Do not choose an institution merely because it is powerful or familiar. For the cross-domain check, quorum exists when present members ≥ the stated threshold.
Task.
Should the request go first to the Local Court or the School Board? Why? Cross-domain check: is quorum met?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Identify the action: decide a dispute under law. 2. Find the role whose definition contains that function: Local Court. 3. School Board has a different stated role, so it is not the first match. Cross-domain check: compare 14 with 8; 14≥8 is true.
Answer.
The request should go first to the Local Court. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.
Knowledge takeaway.
Institutional reasoning is role matching, not guessing which body is “most important.”
Formal model.
Bipartite relation between actions and authorized institutional roles.
